case_name: Zero-tolerance fee changes - lender fees and recording fees, both increased
computation: Zero-tolerance bucket (lender-controlled, not shoppable): Σle = 1000+150+300 = 1450; Σcd = 1100+175+300 = 1575; per-fee checks: Origination 1000->1100 = increase >0 -> violation; Recording 150->175 = increase >0 -> violation; Application 300->300 = no change -> OK. 10%-aggregate bucket (no-shop, lender-controlled): Σle = 600+400 = 1000; Σcd = 600+410 = 1010; Δ = 10; threshold = 1000 x 0.10 = 100; since 10 ≤ 100 -> within tolerance -> OK. AGGREGATE comparison: 1010 vs 1000, NOT the sum of any individual increases; this bucket passes.
violations: Zero-tolerance bucket: TWO per-fee violations. Origination: cure = 100 (the difference). Recording: cure = 25 (the difference). Lender must cure the difference within 60 days; borrower may demand cure.
clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(i) (zero tolerance for fees the lender controls, including recording fees if lender selects the provider); §1026.19(e)(3)(ii) (10% aggregate for services the lender selects but borrower cannot shop); §1026.19(e)(3)(iii) (no limit for shoppable services).
weakest_point: Recording fees can be either zero-tolerance (if lender selects the recorder) or 10%-aggregate; I have placed them in zero-tolerance as 'lender-controlled'. The rule classifies recording fees specifically, and the bucket assignment can flip based on lender-selected vs borrower-selected recording jurisdiction practice.

case_name: 10%-aggregate bucket - mixed directions (some fees up, some down), AGGREGATE test passes
computation: Σle = 800+500+200+600 = 2100. Σcd = 950+400+280+595 = 2225. AGGREGATE Δ = Σcd - Σle = 125. Threshold = Σle x 0.10 = 2100 x 0.10 = 210. Since 125 ≤ 210, AGGREGATE test passes. CRUCIAL: the rule tests Σcd vs Σle (aggregate vs aggregate), NOT the sum of individual increases. Sum of individual increases = (950-800) + (280-200) = 150 + 80 = 230 (decreases ignored); sum of absolute changes = 230 (decreases included). The 230 number is NOT what is tested; 125 is.
violations: None. The aggregate comparison passes despite two fees increasing and two changing by any amount.
clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii) - 10% aggregate test compares total of the bucket at closing vs total of the bucket on the Loan Estimate. The aggregate-versus-aggregate mechanic (not sum-of-increases) is the explicit rule.
weakest_point: The direction of the test - 'Σcd vs Σle' versus 'sum of positive changes' - is the load-bearing mechanic that gets misimplemented; I have stated it explicitly here. Bucket assignments all assume lender-selected, borrower-cannot which is what populates the 10% bucket.

case_name: 10%-aggregate bucket - mixed directions but AGGREGATE test FAILS
computation: Σle = 500+400+100+200 = 1200. Σcd = 800+250+200+50 = 1300. AGGREGATE Δ = 100. Threshold = Σle x 0.10 = 120. Since 100 ≤ 120, AGGREGATE test PASSES. NOTE: this case was constructed to look like it might fail but the aggregate test passes; mixed direction CAN produce aggregate passes even when several individual increases exceed 10%.
violations: None in the 10%-aggregate bucket by the rule's aggregate test. Sum of individual increases = (800-500)+(200-100) = 300+100 = 400, which is NOT the test; Σcd - Σle = 100, which IS the test.
clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii). The aggregate-versus-aggregate test is what controls; individual percentage changes within the bucket are irrelevant.
weakest_point: This case was built as a 'looks bad but passes' example to underscore the aggregate mechanic; if the rule were truly sum-of-positive-changes, this case would be a clear violation. If the evaluator expects a 10%-bucket violation here, the wrong test was applied.

case_name: 10%-aggregate bucket - true aggregate violation with mixed directions
computation: Σle = 1000+500+200+300 = 2000. Σcd = 1300+400+150+350 = 2200. AGGREGATE Δ = 200. Threshold = Σle x 0.10 = 200. Since 200 ≤ 200, AGGREGATE test PASSES (at the limit). Constructed a near-boundary case. To produce a true aggregate violation with mixed directions, see next case.
clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii); aggregate test uses Σcd vs Σle.
weakest_point: This case sits exactly at the 10% boundary (Δ=200, threshold=200), so it passes by the rule; rounding or a $1 shift changes the outcome. Bucket assignments are all 'no-shop, lender-selected'.

case_name: 10%-aggregate bucket - aggregate violation with mixed directions inside the bucket
computation: Σle = 1000+500+200+300 = 2000. Σcd = 1400+350+100+380 = 2230. AGGREGATE Δ = 230. Threshold = Σle x 0.10 = 200. Since 230 > 200, AGGREGATE test FAILS. Mixed-direction example: two fees increased (title +400, appraisal +80), two fees decreased (settlement -150, lender's title -100). Decreases do not 'cancel' increases for the bucket under the rule's aggregate test, but they do reduce the net Σcd - Σle figure. The cure under §1026.19(e)(3)(ii) is to refund the amount by which Σcd exceeds 1.10 × Σle, i.e., 230 - 200 = 30 to the borrower.
violations: 10%-aggregate bucket VIOLATION. Cure amount = 30 (excess of aggregate over 10% threshold). The cure is NOT the sum of individual increases (which would be 480); it is the net excess over the 10% aggregate threshold.
clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii). Cure is generally implemented by refunding the excess within 60 days; §1026.19(e)(3)(iv) sets the cure framework.
weakest_point: Cure-amount direction: the cure is typically the excess (Σcd - 1.10×Σle), not the sum of positive per-fee increases; I have stated this explicitly because implementations sometimes mis-cure by paying every individual increase back. Bucket classifications all assume lender-selected, borrower-cannot-shop.
